history.title: Equal Groups Week

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Multiplication is not a new kind of number. It is a faster way to count something you already know how to count.

1. Read **What Times Really Means**.
2. Learn the words in **Multiplication Words**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Study the **Three Ways to See It** chart.
4. Sort the cards in **Equal Groups or Not?** — the tricky ones are on purpose.
5. Work through **Group Problems**. Draw before you multiply.
6. Take **Multiplication Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember What Times Means**.
8. Read **Multiplication Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Investigation: The Array Around You**.

Bring one photo or drawing of equal groups you found somewhere real. ✖️

Picture panels: Equal groups have meaning; Arrays reveal structure; Use known facts; Check before multiplying. Each enclosed set or row is one group. Count actual objects, not their decorative parts. For this introductory model, use one group count times one common group size only when group sizes match. Unequal collections can still be totaled by addition, regrouping, or combining multiplication and addition. Captions provide mathematical notation; artwork contains no text.

history.title: What Times Really Means
history.data:
## What Times Really Means

You already know how to find 4 + 4 + 4. Multiplication is just a shorter way to write that.

When you see **4 × 3**, read it out loud as **four groups of three**. Not "four three." Four groups of three. The first number tells you how many groups. The second number tells you how many are in each group. The answer, 12, is called the **product**.

There is one rule that makes all of this work, and it is easy to skip past. **The groups have to be equal.**

Imagine three plates. One has 2 crackers, one has 5, and one has 1. Can you multiply? No. You have to add: 2 + 5 + 1 = 8. Multiplication has nothing to grab onto, because there is no "how many in each group" to name.

Now imagine three plates with 4 crackers on every one. That you can multiply. 3 × 4 = 12. The equal groups are what let you take the shortcut.

### The same thing, drawn as a rectangle

An **array** is equal groups lined up in rows and columns. Three rows of 4 chairs is an array. You can count the chairs one at a time and get 12, or you can multiply and get 12 faster.

Arrays show you something surprising. Turn the array of 3 rows of 4 on its side. Now it is 4 rows of 3. Nothing was added or taken away, so the total cannot have changed. It is 12 either way.

That means **3 × 4 and 4 × 3 give the same product.** This is worth more than it looks. If you know 3 × 8, you also know 8 × 3 for free. Every fact you learn comes with a second one attached.

### Using a fact you already know

Say you get stuck on 9 × 6. You may already know 10 × 6 = 60, because tens are easy. Nine groups is one group less than ten groups. So take one group of 6 away: 60 − 6 = 54.

You did not memorise anything new. You leaned on a fact you had and moved one step.

That is really the whole idea. Multiplication counts equal groups fast, and the facts you know can carry you to the ones you do not.

history.title: Group Problems

problems.question: There are 4 tables. Each table has 6 markers. How many markers are there in all?

steps.explanation: Check that the groups are equal. Every table has 6, so they are.
Say it in words: four groups of six. That is 4 x 6.

problems.question: A classroom has 3 rows of chairs with 8 chairs in each row. How many chairs is that?

steps.explanation: Rows and columns that match means this is an array.
Three groups of eight is 3 x 8.
3 x 8 = 24. And turning it sideways would give 8 x 3, which is also 24.

problems.question: You know that 5 x 7 = 35. Without counting anything, what is 7 x 5?

steps.explanation: Picture the array for 5 x 7 and turn it on its side.
Turning it does not add or remove anything, so the total stays put.
So 7 x 5 = 35, the same answer you already had.

problems.question: Juice boxes come in packs of 4. You buy 6 packs. How many juice boxes do you have?

steps.explanation: Every pack holds the same amount, so the groups are equal.
Six groups of four is 6 x 4.

problems.question: What is 9 x 6? Use a fact you already know instead of counting.

steps.explanation: Nine groups is one group fewer than ten groups, and one group here is 6.
So take that group away: 60 - 6 = 54. So 9 x 6 = 54.

problems.question: There are 3 plates. One has 2 crackers, one has 5, and one has 1. How many crackers are there, and can you multiply to find out?
problems.answer: 8 crackers, and no, you cannot multiply

steps.explanation: Check the groups first. They hold 2, 5 and 1, so they are not equal.
With unequal groups there is no how-many-in-each-group to multiply by.

history.title: Multiplication Check

questions.question: What does 5 x 3 mean?
options: Five and three side by side

questions.question: What has to be true before you can multiply to find a total?
options: The numbers have to be small
The groups have to be equal
There have to be exactly two groups
The answer has to be even
questions.correctAnswer: The groups have to be equal

questions.question: In an array, what is a row?
options: A line going up and down

questions.question: You know 6 x 7 = 42. What is 7 x 6?
Three bags hold 3, 6 and 2 marbles. What should you do to find the total?
Which is a good way to work out 9 x 4?
options: Find 10 x 4, then take just 1 away
Find 10 x 4, then take one group of 4 away
Add 9 + 4 and then double the answer
Find 5 x 4 and then double the answer
questions.correctAnswer: Find 10 x 4, then take one group of 4 away

questions.question: Draw or describe an array for 4 x 5. Then say what fact you also know for free, and why.
questions.expectedAnswer: An array with 4 rows of 5, or 5 rows of 4, totalling 20. The free fact is 5 x 4 = 20, because turning the array on its side swaps the rows and columns without adding or removing anything, so the total has to stay the same.

questions.question: A friend says 6 x 3 means six and three. What would you tell them?
questions.expectedAnswer: It means six groups of three, not six and three. Six and three sounds like adding, which would give 9. Six groups of three gives 18, because there are six separate groups with three in each one.

reflections.text: Which multiplication fact do you know best? Why do you think that one stuck?
Where have you seen an array outside of maths?

history.title: Multiplication Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Do I have to memorise all the facts? 😰
data.answer: Eventually you will know most of them by heart, and that does help. But knowing what the fact means comes first. A student who understands groups can rebuild a forgotten fact. A student who only memorised is stuck when it slips.

data.question: Why is anything times zero equal to zero? 🤔
data.answer: Read it as groups of. Four groups of zero means four empty plates, so nothing at all. Zero groups of four means you never got any plates out. Either way the total is nothing.

data.question: Does the order really never matter?
data.answer: For the answer, it never matters: 3 x 8 and 8 x 3 both give 24. For the story, it can matter a lot. Three bags of eight sweets is a different picture from eight bags of three, even though you end up with the same pile.

data.question: What is the easiest times table? ✋
data.answer: Most people find tens easiest, then fives, then twos. That is useful, because you can reach harder facts from easy ones. Nine groups is just ten groups with one group taken back off.

data.question: Can you multiply things that are not objects?
data.answer: Yes. Six days of 20 minutes of reading is 6 x 20 minutes. Anything that comes in equal amounts can be multiplied, including time, money and distance.

data.question: Why do we even need multiplication if we can just add? ⏱️
data.answer: You can always add, and it will work. But adding 20 groups of 7 means writing 20 numbers and making 19 chances to slip. Multiplication does the same job in one step.

history.title: Investigation: The Array Around You
history.meta: 3rd Grade • Investigation brief • find real arrays, write both facts

data.title: The Array Around You
data.instructions: Find real things arranged in equal groups or rows. Write the multiplication for each one, both ways round. Then find one thing that looks like an array but is not.
data.fitReason: Arrays are genuinely everywhere and students walk past them all day without seeing the maths. Hunting for real ones, and being required to find a near-miss, forces the equal-groups rule to be used as a test rather than repeated as a phrase.

brief.context: Your classroom, your school and your home are full of things in rows and equal groups. Window panes. Floor tiles. Egg cartons. Muffin trays. Lockers. Chairs. You may draw them or take a photo of them.
brief.audience: The class, who will build a wall of real arrays with the facts written under each one
brief.drivingQuestion: Where are the equal groups hiding in the places I go every day?
brief.seedDirection: Start with something in straight rows. Those are the easiest to count. Then look for the harder kind, where the groups match but are not lined up.
lockedLessonFacts: The first number tells you how many groups, and the second how many are in each group.
The groups have to be equal or you cannot multiply.
An array is equal groups lined up in rows and columns.
Turning an array on its side gives the same product.
openQuestions: Which was harder to find, an array or a near-miss?
Did anyone find the same object but count it a different way?
Is there a shape that is almost an array but has one row wrong?
stakeholders: Your class, who will check your counting
A student who still reads the times sign as and
Your teacher, who will use your wall next year
criteria: At least four real arrays or equal groups, each one drawn or photographed
Both facts written under every one
The product worked out, then checked by a partner
At least one near-miss that is not equal, with a sentence saying why it fails
constraints: The things have to be real and findable, not invented
Under 60 words of writing on the whole page
brief.deliverable: A page for the class wall. Show at least four real arrays. Write both facts and the product under each one. Then add one near-miss, with a sentence on why you cannot multiply it.

parallelExample.context: A student photographed the muffin tray at home, 3 rows of 4.
parallelExample.move: She wrote 3 x 4 = 12 and 4 x 3 = 12 under it. Then she found the cutlery drawer, with 6 forks, 5 spoons and 4 knives, and wrote that it looked like groups but could not be multiplied because the groups were different sizes.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: The near-miss is what proved she understood the rule. Anyone can spot a grid, but only someone using the rule notices a set of groups that fails it.
